title: Cop whose gun killed Eric Osawe tells inquest he wishes he'd been shot himself
subtitle: Const. David Cavanagh, who was exonerated in the death of Etobicoke resident Eric Osawe, said Wednesday that the incident has stayed with him. Osawe's mother was unmoved.
article: Six years after David Cavanagh's MP5 sub-machine gun fired and killed 26-year-old Eric Osawe, the Toronto police constable says he wishes the bullets had hit him instead.

"There hasn't been a day that's gone by that I (didn't) wish that round went through my leg," Cavanagh said Wednesday, testifying at a coroner's inquest into Osawe's death . "There hasn't been a day gone by that I wasn't thinking about what occurred."

The incident occurred in the early morning hours of Sept. 29, 2010 as ETF officers executed a search warrant of Osawe's Etobicoke apartment. Osawe, who police knew to have a violent past, was thought to be in possession of a firearm and drugs.

Cavanagh's gun fired while he and three other officers attempted to handcuff Osawe, who was struck by one bullet to the spine and died within 15 seconds. An Ontario court judge deemed the shot accidental.
Osawe's mother Magdeline said she didn't find Cavanagh's testimony sincere.

"Somebody died. If I hear this in 2010, that's a different issue," she said. "But we are hearing it after six years, so as a parent, how will you feel all of a sudden if (the) officer that killed your son is telling you a different story? It doesn't make sense to me."
The officer recalled a "very violent, chaotic struggle" with Osawe leading up to the gunshot. He said Osawe resisted when officers found him on his bed, his hands partially hidden.

Cavanagh ordered Osawe to get on the ground, where he figured he could most easily take control and handcuff him. But Osawe didn't respond to demands, and instead held a "neutral, unsurprised look" on his face, which Cavanagh thought might mean he was forming a plan to resist arrest, possibly using a gun of his own.
As Cavanagh got closer, he decided to go "hands-on" and used his right thumb to put his gun into the safety position, before releasing it from his hands into a sling attached to his vest.

Osawe resisted by punching, pushing and grabbing as the officer grabbed his arm in attempt to get him on the floor, according to Cavanagh. He and another officer managed to pull Osawe off his bed. He ended up face down, still "pulling" at Cavanagh, who said his own weapon had been jostled around during struggle.
"It was like a mechanical bull. He was thrashing around on the floor," Cavanagh said.

Cavanagh said he next saw Osawe reaching under his dresser and seemed like he was looking for something, possibly a gun. The officer lunged over Osawe's body with both hands to get a hold of his reaching arm and heard a "muffled pop."
He saw blood coming from a toonie-sized hole on the back of Osawe's clothing and then noticed his gun, hanging from the sling attached to his vest, was in semi-automatic mode.

The officer speculates two things must have happened leading to the accidental discharge: that the safety of his gun had been turned back off at some point during the struggle with Osawe due to tugging and punching, and that the trigger got caught with a piece of equipment he was carrying on his vest.
"As much as I wish I could clinically recreate that struggle with accuracy, it's impossible," he said.
Coroner's inquests are held not to assign blame but to probe the circumstances surrounding a death and formulate recommendations to prevent future fatalities.

Cavanagh, who left the ETF shortly after the incident but is still a Toronto police officer, said the only thing he'd change if he could redo what happened was the type of sling he wore for his weapon.
At the time, officers had the choice of wearing a Y sling or an H&K sling. A gun attached to a Y sling is easier to manoeuvre than one in an H&K, , witnesses told the inquest on Tuesday .
Cavanagh said he wore a Y sling during the 2010 incident, but thinks had he worn an H&K sling instead, its angle and its lack of flexibility may have prevented his gun from shooting Osawe.
Sgt. Michael Forestell, an ETF training officer, testified Wednesday that the H&K sling is now the only one issued to ETF officers carrying MP5 guns.

The court heard that there have been four other incidents involving accidental discharges of MP5s since 1997. Forestell said officers are now trained to be aware of accidental shots that can result when a safety switch is unknowingly flicked. He said constantly checking the safety is the best practice.
In a tearful plea outside the courthouse, Osawe's mother said she hoped this inquest will ensure "other mothers will not experience what I went through."
